newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Will Deng's death upset balance in Taiwan strait?.
newsitem.headline: Will Deng's death upset balance in Taiwan strait?.

text.p: In Deng Xiaoping's China, no task was more important than hoisting the red communist five-star over the long-estranged territories of Taiwan and Hong Kong.
Though he did not live to see it, Deng brokered the historic 1984 deal under which Britain will cede Hong Kong back to China on July 1, ending more than a century of colonial rule.
The future of Nationalist-ruled Taiwan remains cloudier.
Deng's death late on Wednesday opens up new questions for the hugely wealthy and increasingly democratic capitalist enclave lying just off China's southeast coast.
Will Deng's successors have the same ardour for reunification now that Deng is gone?
Will Deng's death embolden Taiwanese who bitterly oppose unification and pine to replace Taiwan's exiled Republic of China with their own indepedendent Republic of Taiwan?
Or does his passing open the door to fresh approaches by Taiwan forces who desire more intimate links with the mainland?
Experts and officials said little would change soon.
"At this sensitive moment, it is unlikely Taiwan will do something stupid to infuriate the Chinese communists," said National Taiwan University political scientist Chang Lin-chen.

"Basically, relations between the two sides of the Taiwan Strait should remain more or less the same," Huang Yao-yu, director of the mainland affairs department of the Nationalist Party, told reporters.
Huang affirmed that Beijing still sets the basic ground rules for Taiwan with its standing vow to take the island by force if it pursues independence.
"As long as we stay away from the splittist road, the Chinese communists are unlikely to send forces to attack us," Huang said.
Taiwan and China split after a civil war ended in 1949, with the vanquished Nationalists taking refuge on the island.

Taiwan's government vowed to continue seeking dialogue with Beijing but said Taipei stood by its view that democratic political reforms on the mainland and a renunciation of force must precede reunification.
In the meantime, China must respect Taiwan's need for "survival and development space" and the "basic right to participate in international activities".
Forces on opposing sides of the bitter reunification debate were as divided as ever.

The New Party, formed by Nationalist dissidents frustrated with the ruling party's go-slow policy on reunification, called on President Lee Teng-hui to go to Beijing for Deng's funeral -- and hold unprecedented talks with Chinese president Jiang Zemin.
"This will not only provide a chance for leaders of the two sides to meet, but also help ease strained relations," said New Party chief Chen Kuai-miao.
"Deng's death gives strained Taiwan-mainland relations a new chance for an easing of tension," he said.
Chiu Yi-jen, secretary-general of the independence-minded Democratic Progressive Party, said Deng's death changed nothing.

"We will not abandon our pro-independence policy, but we are not going to push the limit and provoke the Chinese communists at this time," Chiu told Reuters. The party, Taiwan's main opposition, helped foster democracy and bring down martial law in 1987 with its outright advocacy of independence in the 1980s, but more recently has toned down such calls in the face of China's hardening line.
China mounted months of sabre-rattling war games and missile tests near Taiwan in 1995 and 1996 to warn the island not to stray from the Nationalists' longstanding pro-unification stand.

Experts said uncertainty over China's transition to the post-Deng era ensured the Nationalists would not seize the moment to launch fresh moves to assert its sovereignty -- something sure to provoke Beijing.

On Beijing's part, China's leaders would focus on the transition and not tinker with Deng's "one country, two systems" model for bringing Taiwan and Hong Kong under Beijing's rule, political analysts said.
"The future leadership will continue the peaceful unification process or formula...unless Taiwan does some political action that intimidates China," Taiwan military analyst Andrew Young told Reuters.
